channel.title: Daily Digest
channel.description: Curated tech blog summaries, inspired by Andrej Karpathy's reading list

item.title: Show your hands honor for the strange power they bring you
item.description: This article explores the design of intuitive and ergonomic finger-based interactions for digital interfaces. It offers extensive practical guidance, including 38 interactive playgrounds to help designers create more natural user experiences.

item.title: You don’t understand, prices can’t go down
item.description: The article critiques how modern economic policies prioritize inflating asset prices over genuine productivity, leading to a disconnect between market valuations and reality. It argues that the systemic refusal to allow prices to fall creates dangerous bubbles and transfers wealth from productive activities to speculative endeavors.

item.title: GLM 5.2 playing text adventures
item.description: The author evaluates the performance of the new GLM 5.2 open-weights model by pitting it against Gemini 3 Flash in text-adventure games. The analysis utilizes a consistent benchmarking harness to measure success based on achievement counts within a fixed budget.

item.title: Open Source vs the Invisible Hand
item.description: The article explores the contradiction between traditional economic theory and the reality of open source software production. It argues that open source ignores market axioms like the free rider problem and price-based quality signaling to create a highly functional, massive ecosystem of public goods.

item.title: Why doesn’t Get­Last­Input­Info() return info for the user I’m impersonating?
item.description: The GetLastInputInfo() function does not track activity for impersonated users because it is not designed to account for impersonation contexts. The API behavior is tied to the physical input state rather than the specific security token being used.

item.title: Windows stack limit checking retrospective, follow-up
item.description: This post is a follow-up discussion regarding the technical implementation of stack limit checking in Windows. It specifically examines the choices involved in selecting CPU registers to manage stack allocation sizes.

item.title: I hate compilers
item.description: The author humorously challenges the expectation that compilers always produce deterministic output from identical source code. The post highlights the complexities and often frustrating nuances that cause non-deterministic behavior in compilation processes.

item.title: Book Review: The Great When by Alan Moore ★★★★☆
item.description: This review of Alan Moore's 'The Great When' highlights the author's exceptionally ornate and polysyllabic prose style. The reviewer praises the book's descriptive language, noting that while it is heavily overwritten, the stylistic execution creates a delightful reading experience.

item.title: Pluralistic: AI digital sovereignty risk doesn't exist (18 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow argues that the concept of 'AI digital sovereignty' is a logical fallacy, similar to his critique of blockchain-based institutions. He contends that just as DAOs still require human intermediaries to act in the physical world, AI-driven solutions often fail to eliminate the human trust-based dependencies they claim to solve.

item.title: ‘Popa’ Botnet Linked to Publicly-Traded Israeli Firm
item.description: Security researchers have linked the 'Popa' Android botnet, which has compromised millions of consumer TV boxes for illegal activities, to NetNut, a residential proxy provider owned by the Israeli firm Alarum Technologies. This discovery highlights the abuse of proxy networks for malicious operations like ad fraud and data scraping.

item.title: GLM-5.2 is probably the most powerful text-only open weights LLM
item.description: Z.ai has released GLM-5.2, a 753B parameter Mixture of Experts model that currently stands as a leading open-weights LLM. Despite its impressive benchmark performance and 1 million token context window, the model is noted for being significantly more token-hungry than its competitors.

item.title: Maybe it's time for lots of little indie AIs to take over
item.description: Anil Dash advocates for a shift away from massive AI models toward a ecosystem of smaller, independent, and responsible AI players. He critiques the current influence of corrupt corporate and political interests, suggesting that systemic coercion forces widespread adoption despite user skepticism.

item.title: Summoning the Demon
item.description: The article critiques the development of AI as a reflection of societal flaws rather than a technological inevitability. It argues that the current pursuit of AI optimization is a self-destructive path that will eventually lead to systemic collapse and social transformation.

item.title: Logic for Programmers v0.15, Livecoding
item.description: The author announces that 'Logic for Programmers' version 0.15 is the final release candidate before the 1.0 print edition. Additionally, the post highlights two music livecoding languages, Strudel and CLAVIER-36, discussed at a recent Chicago meetup.

item.title: You Got Faster. Your Company Didn’t.
item.description: Individual productivity gains from AI often fail to translate into company-wide success. Instead of true value creation, these gains frequently manifest as shifting the burden of slow processes onto other team members.

item.title: Formalizing a ring theorem with Lean 4 and Claude
item.description: John D. Cook explores using Claude to generate Lean 4 code for formalizing mathematical proofs. The article documents the author's efforts to verify specific theorems, highlighting both the potential and the practical challenges of using AI assistants for formal verification.

item.title: Retrofitting the WM_COPY­DATA message onto Windows 3.1
item.description: This post discusses the historical implementation of the WM_COPYDATA message within the Windows 3.1 operating system. It highlights how the feature was intentionally engineered for simplicity.

item.title: Pluralistic: The (real) dead economy theory (17 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: This article examines the 'dead economy' theory, arguing that financial markets no longer accurately value assets. It cites Elon Musk's post-2020 commercial failures alongside the mainstream adoption of volatile assets like cryptocurrency as evidence of institutional failure.

item.title: Quoting Charity Majors
item.description: Charity Majors highlights how generative AI has fundamentally altered software development economics, making code production nearly instantaneous and essentially free. This shift transitions code from a high-value asset to a disposable commodity, necessitating a greater focus on engineering discipline.

item.title: <click-to-play> — a still that plays
item.description: Simon Willison introduces a web component that converts animated GIFs into still frames, only loading the animation when a user interacts with it. This technique optimizes page performance by preventing large GIF files from loading automatically.

item.title: NetNewsWire Status
item.description: This post highlights Brent Simmons' work on NetNewsWire, an open-source RSS reader he has been perfecting in his retirement. The author praises the project for its quality and independence from commercial pressure, noting its status as an indispensable tool for reading.

item.title: datasette 1.0a34
item.description: Datasette 1.0a34 introduces long-awaited features that allow users to insert, edit, and delete rows directly through the web interface. Inspired by development work on Datasette Agent, this update bridges the gap between chat-based SQL interaction and the standard UI.

item.title: datasette-tailscale 0.1a0
item.description: Simon Willison has released an experimental alpha plugin, datasette-tailscale, which allows users to host a Datasette server directly on their Tailnet. By utilizing the tailscale-rs library, the plugin provides a simplified way to expose local data via a private Tailscale network.

item.title: Key, in sight
item.description: This comprehensive guide explores the intricacies of mechanical keyboard customization. It serves as an extensive resource for enthusiasts looking to refine their typing experience through hardware modifications.

item.title: Lean Launch Pad 2026 @ Stanford – Lessons Learned Presentations
item.description: Steve Blank reflects on the 16th annual Lean LaunchPad course at Stanford, tracing its evolution from a radical startup methodology to an industry standard. The post highlights the enduring impact of teaching evidence-based entrepreneurship to the next generation of founders.

item.title: Do not invite big-tech to join your digital autonomy discussion
item.description: The author reflects on the irony of inviting big-tech companies to participate in discussions about European digital autonomy. While acknowledging that these corporations will remain part of the future business landscape, he argues that their presence undermines the goal of achieving genuine independence.

item.title: The Sword Juggling Fallacy
item.description: The author uses the analogy of sword juggling to illustrate the difference between a language being 'simple' versus 'easy.' While C has a small, simple syntax, the author argues that writing correct code in C is extremely difficult due to complex memory management and pointer safety.

item.title: Ada Palmer – Machiavelli is the most misunderstood thinker of all time
item.description: Historian Ada Palmer argues that Machiavelli is frequently misinterpreted and that his complex relationship with power was shaped by intense personal suffering. The discussion sheds light on why a man who was tortured by a regime would ultimately seek to serve it.

item.title: Lean, not backpressure
item.description: The author critiques the use of 'backpressure' to describe systems handling AI-generated code, arguing that the term implies slowing down rather than changing quality standards. Instead, the author proposes 'lean manufacturing' as a more accurate analogy for managing unstable, high-volume inputs.

item.title: How Open Source Projects Change Hands
item.description: This article explores the mechanisms and vulnerabilities surrounding the transfer of open-source project maintainership. It examines various methods of succession, from personal handoffs and GitHub account settings to formal registry adoption processes, highlighting the lack of robust infrastructure for project continuity.

item.title: Partial fraction decomposition
item.description: Partial fraction decomposition is primarily taught in calculus as a technique for integrating rational functions by breaking them into simpler, integrable terms. This post highlights how the concept is often treated narrowly in classrooms and implies broader applications beyond simple integration.

item.title: Three examples suffice
item.description: This article discusses the mathematical principle that while finite examples are usually insufficient to prove a theorem, there are specific contexts where they suffice. The author uses the relationship between pentagonal and triangular numbers to illustrate how numerical patterns can be verified through concrete examples.

item.title: Testing pentagonal numbers
item.description: This post explains the formula for calculating pentagonal numbers and introduces the concept of generalized pentagonal numbers. It explores the mathematical properties of these sequences and how to compute them for both positive and non-positive integers.

item.title: The time the x86 emulator team found code so bad that they fixed it during emulation
item.description: This post discusses a specific instance where the x86 emulator team encountered exceptionally poor code. To ensure system stability and performance, the team implemented real-time fixes during the emulation process.

item.title: Two Way TV - product photos of 1997's hottest gadget
item.description: The author reflects on their 1990s experience with 'Two Way TV,' an early interactive television experiment from the BBC. This post provides a nostalgic look at the hardware and functionality of the forgotten technology used to play along with live game shows.

item.title: Debugging on Prod
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The author recounts their struggle debugging a production-only error triggered by AI-generated refactoring code. The issue was eventually identified as an infinite recursion bug within a third-party Markdown library that behaved unexpectedly due to environment differences.

item.title: Quoting Georgi Gerganov
item.description: Georgi Gerganov shares his practical experience using the Qwen3.6-27B model for daily coding maintenance tasks. He describes his lightweight workflow using an offline agent and custom system prompts to align the model with his personal coding style.

item.title: The Fable 5 Export Controls Harm US Cyber Defense
item.description: The article critiques current export controls that misidentify defensive AI code-fixing capabilities as dangerous jailbreaks. It argues that banning models for their ability to patch vulnerabilities hinders essential cybersecurity work rather than preventing actual cyber attacks.

item.title: Quoting Matteo Wong, The Atlantic
item.description: This post highlights an excerpt from The Atlantic regarding Anthropic's engagement with cybersecurity experts to evaluate AI safety. It demonstrates how models can be prompted to perform security tasks while navigating jailbreak restrictions through specific framing.

item.title: Cloudflare CAPTCHA on at least one ampersand
item.description: The author demonstrates how to refine Cloudflare WAF rules to prevent false positives when protecting a search engine. By modifying the rule to trigger only when the URL query contains an ampersand, legitimate single-term searches can bypass the CAPTCHA.

item.title: datasette-agent 0.3a0
item.description: Datasette-agent version 0.3a0 introduces the execute_write_sql tool, enabling AI agents to perform database write operations securely. The update adds a mandatory user approval mechanism for data modifications and expands support for these interactive confirmations within the chat terminal.

item.title: A brief history of KV cache compression developments
item.description: This article explores the evolution of KV cache compression techniques, including MQA, GQA, and MLA. It highlights how these architectural innovations have been essential in enabling the long context windows required for modern agentic LLMs.

item.title: Things that made me think: Open Source trust relationships, knowledge without provenance, and theory building
item.source: Tom Renner on My place to put things
item.description: This blog post explores the intersection of technology and human behavior, examining how AI impacts trust in open-source ecosystems and knowledge provenance. The author reflects on the necessity of new systems to verify AI outputs and redefines programming as a continuous process of theory building rather than mere code production.

item.title: Weekly Update 508
item.description: The author reflects on the frustration of finding light switches that are both aesthetically pleasing and offer specific functional requirements like push-button operation. This post highlights the difficulties in sourcing simple home hardware that meets modern design and usability standards.

item.title: EU & Civil Society need to progress on Digital Autonomy
item.description: The article argues that current discussions on digital autonomy are stalling and often revolve around rhetoric rather than actionable progress. It calls for civil society and think tanks to broaden their focus beyond legislative frameworks and European values to address the long-term, practical challenges of digital sovereignty.

item.title: Quaternion Rotations, Claude, and Lean
item.description: The author tests Claude's ability to identify a mathematical typo in a previous blog post regarding quaternion and rotation matrix conversions. The post highlights the potential for AI models to assist in proofreading technical content and mathematical derivations.

item.title: Writing Prolog with ChatGPT
item.description: The author explores using ChatGPT to solve a logic puzzle by generating Prolog code. The post evaluates the model's ability to handle constraints on a 4x4 chessboard compared to previous experiments with Claude.

item.title: [RSS Club] What happens to old posts?
item.description: The article discusses the nature of 'RSS Club' posts, which are exclusive content accessible only to RSS feed subscribers. It addresses the challenge of permanent access for readers who bookmark these posts but later find them inaccessible or restricted.

item.title: Did Frank Sinatra really think "Something" was a Lennon/McCartney song?
item.description: The author investigates the persistent claim that Frank Sinatra famously misattributed The Beatles' song 'Something' to Lennon and McCartney. By analyzing the origins of this anecdote, the post treats it as an apocryphal myth similar to other common music industry misconceptions.

item.title: Arp 185:
item.description: This post presents an amateur astrophotography capture of the galaxy Arp 185, including technical details of the equipment, exposure settings, and processing steps. The author discusses the galaxy's structural classification and notes the presence of a background galaxy.

item.title: Pluralistic: AI and amateurism (15 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow reflects on his lifelong journey with computing and AI, addressing why his deep technical background hasn't made him an AI booster. He explores the concept of amateurism in the context of generative technology and criticizes current industry trends.

item.title: "They screwed us": Personality clashes sent Anthropic's models offline
item.description: This post discusses the internal conflict and diplomatic tensions between Anthropic and the US government regarding the suspension of its AI models, Mythos and Fable. It highlights the difficulty of achieving perfect jailbreak resistance and the ongoing negotiations to restore access to these tools.

item.title: Quoting Julia Evans
item.description: Julia Evans suggests that effective writing is best achieved by targeting a single, specific person, such as one's past self or a friend. This approach helps simplify communication and ensures the content resonates more deeply with the intended reader.

item.title: Why AI hasn’t replaced software engineers, and won’t
item.description: Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue that AI is unlikely to replace software engineers, citing data that shows no mass AI-related layoffs in the tech industry. They identify that the true bottlenecks in software engineering, such as decision-making, verification, and accountability, remain resistant to automation.

item.title: AI GPUs probably live longer than three years
item.description: This article challenges the assumption that AI GPUs have a short, three-year lifespan, suggesting they may remain functional and relevant for longer. It examines the factors contributing to hardware longevity in the context of rapidly evolving artificial intelligence demands.

item.title: Building a serial and VGA "everything console"
item.description: The author outlines their DIY project to build a compact, portable 'everything console' for vintage computing and serial port systems. By repurposing a used laptop and integrating specialized USB-to-serial hardware, they create a versatile terminal solution that avoids the bulk of CRT displays.

item.title: Plugins case study: Pluggy
item.description: This article explores Pluggy, a Python library originally developed for pytest that facilitates building plugin systems. The author explains how to use hooks via decorators to create a modular architecture, demonstrating the concept through a practical implementation of an HTML conversion tool.

item.title: How can I schedule work on a thread pool with low latency?
item.description: This article clarifies that the Windows thread pool is fundamentally optimized for maximizing system throughput rather than achieving low-latency task execution. It warns developers that attempting to use the thread pool for latency-sensitive operations may lead to suboptimal performance.

item.title: Making glass-to-metal seals for home­made vacuum tubes.
item.description: This blog post explores the challenges of creating vacuum-tight glass-to-metal seals for homemade vacuum tubes. It explains the importance of matching thermal expansion coefficients between glass and metal, detailing the author's experiments with copper plating to achieve successful seals.

item.title: Publishing WASM wheels to PyPI for use with Pyodide
item.description: Pyodide now supports publishing Python packages built for WebAssembly (WASM) directly to PyPI, eliminating the need for manual maintenance by core developers. This update allows package maintainers to distribute WASM-compatible wheels just like native platform wheels, significantly improving the ecosystem's scalability.

item.title: luau-wasm 0.1a0
item.description: Simon Willison has released luau-wasm 0.1a0, a tool for running the Luau scripting language via WebAssembly. The release is accompanied by documentation on publishing WASM wheels for use with Pyodide.

item.title: Mapping SQLite result columns back to their source `table.column`
item.description: Simon Willison explores methods for programmatically mapping SQL query result columns back to their original table and column names in SQLite. He leverages AI-assisted research to evaluate various technical approaches, including using the APSW library, Python ctypes to access C-level functions, and analyzing EXPLAIN output.

item.title: Human Routers of Machine Words
item.description: This article explores the concept of individuals acting as 'human routers' for AI, effectively using artificial intelligence as a cognitive extension to organize and process complex thoughts. It highlights how humans integrate machine-generated text into their own intellectual workflows to enhance reasoning and output.

item.title: Reading List 06/13/2026
item.description: This reading list explores diverse engineering and infrastructure topics, ranging from architectural integration of housing and libraries to heavy manufacturing and large-scale geopolitical infrastructure projects. It highlights unique developments in construction, defense, and international transport concepts.

item.title: This Week in Package Management: 13 June 2026
item.description: This weekly digest covers key security updates in package management, including npm v12 breaking changes regarding lifecycle scripts and remote dependencies. It also highlights new features in uv for vulnerability auditing and malware detection, as well as pnpm's hardened bootstrapping process.

item.title: RSA munitions T-shirt
item.description: The article recounts the historical protest by Adam Back in 1995, who printed an obfuscated RSA encryption algorithm on T-shirts to challenge US export restrictions on cryptography. This act highlighted the absurd government classification of code as munitions during the period of strict encryption regulation.

item.title: Dangerous Technology For Americans Only
item.description: The article critiques the US government's export control directives on AI models, noting how Anthropic's 'safety' framing has resulted in restrictions based on nationality rather than objective risk. The author argues that treating AI as a weapon for exclusive American use promotes nationalism and division, serving as a warning to non-US citizens about the geopolitical shift in technology control.

item.title: The adder at the heart of Intel's 8087 floating-point chip
item.description: This article explores the technical design of the 69-bit adder within the Intel 8087 floating-point coprocessor. It details how the chip uses specific architectural innovations to handle complex arithmetic and carry operations efficiently.

item.title: Pluralistic: Shareholder supremacy and the precog CEO (13 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques Milton Friedman's 55-year-old doctrine of shareholder supremacy, which mandates that corporate managers focus exclusively on profit maximization. The article argues that this theory, intended to provide an objective metric for business success, is essentially unfalsifiable and flawed in its premise.

item.title: Statement on the US government directive to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5
item.description: Anthropic has been directed by the US government to suspend access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models due to alleged national security risks related to jailbreaking. The company contests the severity of these concerns, noting that the reported capabilities are already widely available in other models used for security research.

item.title: OpenAI WebRTC Audio Session, now with document context
item.description: Simon Willison has updated his WebRTC audio tool to support OpenAI's latest GPT-Realtime-2 model. Users can now input custom document context to engage in real-time, voice-based conversations about specific textual information directly within their browser.

item.title: I Am Not a Reverse Centaur
item.description: The author discusses the increasing influx of LLM-generated pull requests in open-source projects, which threatens to turn experienced maintainers into 'reverse centaurs'—humans who spend their time reviewing machine-made code. He reaffirms his refusal to rely on LLMs and outlines his approach to maintaining personal agency while managing these contributions.

item.title: This Week on The Analog Antiquarian
item.description: This entry from The Digital Antiquarian explores the early game development history surrounding the title Henry VI, Part 1. It examines the technical and creative context of this specific software release within the broader timeline of early computing history.

item.title: AI will be massively deflationary
item.description: The article argues that anxieties surrounding AI companies like Anthropic are overstated, suggesting that the underlying technology is becoming a commodity. It posits that while these firms may hold grand ideologies, the competitive nature of the industry and economic realities will lead to deflationary effects rather than total control.

item.title: Joint Guidance on Vulnerability Naming and Disclosure
item.description: The Vulnerability Naming Authority has established a standardized, unified process for naming and disclosing vulnerabilities in the United States. This framework introduces centralized registry requirements, including specific branding elements like logos and color palettes, alongside a deconfliction database to ensure unique naming.

item.title: Understanding the rationale behind a rule when trying to circumvent it
item.description: This post reflects on the nuances of following rules versus attempting to circumvent them. It highlights the importance of understanding the underlying rationale of a rule rather than just adhering to its literal technicality.

item.title: Why are cached input tokens cheaper with AI services?
item.description: This article explains why AI services offer lower costs for cached input tokens. It highlights that caching reduces the computational burden on GPUs, as they do not need to perform redundant calculations for previously processed sequences.

item.title: Gadget Review: TP Link EH210 Ethernet Splitter (USB-C) ★★★★★
item.description: This post reviews the TP Link EH210, a compact USB-C Ethernet splitter designed for rooms with limited device requirements. The author evaluates its practical application for simplifying home networking in spaces that do not necessitate a full-sized Ethernet switch.

item.title: Pluralistic: Google's new remote attestation scheme is every bit as terrible as its old remote attestation scheme (12 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow critiques Google's remote attestation schemes, arguing they undermine the fundamental role of browsers as user agents. He emphasizes that browsers must remain interoperable and obedient to the user rather than enforcing manufacturer-dictated restrictions.

item.title: I can never fully embrace LLMs for code
item.source: Software and Tech stories from an Insider - iDiallo.com
item.description: The author reflects on the conflict between the convenience of AI-generated code and the necessity of understanding it. Unlike using established libraries, AI outputs lack vetting and consistency, leading the author to prioritize code comprehension over the speed gains offered by LLMs.

item.title: Quoting Andrew Singleton
item.description: This post features a satirical excerpt from Andrew Singleton's 'AI Economics for Dummies' that critiques the circular and inflated nature of current AI investment models. The piece uses a metaphorical story about a crematorium to highlight the lack of genuine financial substance behind some high-profile AI revenue claims.

item.title: Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive
item.description: Simon Willison shares his experience with the proactive capabilities of Claude Fable 5, specifically in debugging software. He illustrates how the AI independently explores local project dependencies and files to troubleshoot UI glitches based on a simple screenshot and prompt.

item.title: You can finally power on a Mac remotely
item.description: Apple has introduced a new feature allowing users to power on Mac computers remotely, addressing long-standing usability issues. While media reports link this to the controversial M4 Mac mini power button placement, the author highlights its broader utility for server and remote access management.

item.title: Hacking Google with A.I. for $500,000
item.description: The author shares the findings of an extensive security audit conducted by deploying AI to analyze Google's vast infrastructure. The project resulted in identifying numerous vulnerabilities across 1,500 APIs and 3,600 keys, earning the researcher $500,000 in bug bounties.

item.title: My Portable Heater
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.description: The author explores the Gigabyte Aorus RTX 5060 Ti AI Box, an external GPU that bridges the gap between portability and performance. While initially dismissed by gamers for desktop use, its compact design and increased RAM make it a compelling tool for laptop users and AI enthusiasts.

item.title: Biological Evolution and Information Acquisition
item.description: This post discusses a simulation by economist Brian Arthur that models technological evolution. It demonstrates how complex systems can emerge from simple building blocks through the iterative combination of functional components.

item.title: What Happened to tea.xyz
item.description: The article analyzes the decline of tea.xyz, a cryptocurrency project aimed at rewarding open-source maintainers that lost 90% of its value shortly after launch. It examines the project's background, its split into the pkgx package manager and the tea crypto protocol, and the flaws in its Proof of Contribution incentive model.

item.title: Solving a chess puzzle with Claude and Prolog
item.description: This article explores the use of Prolog, a logic programming language, for solving chess puzzles. It discusses the linguistic origins of Prolog and highlights its unique ability to represent logical problems directly while weighing its pros and cons.

item.title: Formally proving a calculation with Claude and Lean
item.description: This post details an experiment using the AI model Claude to generate Lean code for verifying a specific mathematical proof involving Fourier coefficients and Bessel functions. The author explores the potential for large language models to assist in formal mathematical verification.

item.title: What’s the opposite of Clip­Cursor that lets me exclude the cursor from a region?
item.description: The article addresses whether Windows offers a built-in feature to exclude the cursor from a specific region, similar to how ClipCursor restricts it. It clarifies that such a feature does not exist, but suggests that developers can achieve this effect through virtual exclusion.

item.title: Pluralistic: The world has moved on (11 Jun 2026)
item.source: Pluralistic: Daily links from Cory Doctorow
item.description: Cory Doctorow reflects on the generational perspective of technological change and societal complexity, referencing Douglas Adams' famous quote on human attitudes toward innovation. He uses the 'National Customer Rage Survey' to illustrate increasing consumer dissatisfaction, questioning whether current technological frustration is a legitimate critique or merely nostalgic bias.

item.title: datasette 1.0a33
item.description: Datasette 1.0a33 has been released, introducing expanded support for the _extra= pattern to include queries and rows. This update simplifies JSON API interactions and is accompanied by a new, AI-assisted tool for exploring these API features.

item.title: asyncinject 0.7
item.description: Simon Willison released version 0.7 of asyncinject, a utility library designed for asyncio dependency injection. The update includes bug fixes identified and implemented with the help of Claude AI.

item.title: Anthropic Walks Back Policy That Could Have ‘Sabotaged’ AI Researchers Using Claude
item.description: Anthropic has reversed its controversial policy of using invisible safeguards to limit AI research requests within its Claude models. The company apologized for the lack of transparency and committed to making refusal triggers visible to users in future updates.

item.title: datasette-agent 0.2a0
item.description: Datasette-agent 0.2a0 introduces an interactive 'ask_user' feature allowing agents to prompt users for input mid-execution, with conversation state persisted across server restarts. It also adds a 'save_query' tool that enables agents to save SQL queries to Datasette, requiring human approval for security.

item.title: Weekly Update 507
item.description: Troy Hunt reflects on reaching a milestone of 1,000 data breaches tracked on Have I Been Pwned. He highlights the extensive operational, legal, and administrative challenges involved in maintaining such a large-scale security platform beyond just technical data processing.

item.title: Being “Good” at Things
item.description: The author discusses how professional golfer Collin Morikawa redefines what it means to be 'good' at golf. Instead of focusing on arbitrary numerical scores, true proficiency is defined by consistency, honesty, and finishing every hole according to the rules.

item.title: Nontrailing separators do not spark joy
item.description: The article discusses the inconvenience of non-trailing separators in programming languages and data formats like JSON. It argues that prohibiting trailing commas complicates version control diffs and code refactoring by forcing unnecessary changes to surrounding lines.

item.title: Pulling on a thread
item.description: John D. Cook explores how seemingly unrelated blog posts often share underlying mathematical connections. He highlights his recent investigation into a specific numerical approximation, demonstrating how curiosity leads to deeper analytical threads.

item.title: Gaslighting Openness
item.description: The author argues that large tech companies are increasingly using 'safety' and 'security' narratives to restrict user access to data and AI models. He emphasizes that maintaining open access and supporting regulations like the EU's DMA is crucial for preventing corporate consolidation and preserving democratized technology.
